title: What Is Stress-Strain Curve?
summary: …and how to calculate it in every material
body_text: How Do You Read a Stress-Strain Graph? Read stress on the vertical axis and strain on the horizontal axis to understand material performance. Start at the origin, where both values are zero, and follow the line upward. The initial straight section shows the elastic region where the material recovers its shape. The steepness of the line indicates the stiffness of the material. Locate the yield point where the line begins to curve, marking the start of permanent deformation. The plastic region follows, showing how the material stretches under continued load. Find the highest point on the curve, which represents the ultimate tensile strength. The curve drops toward the fracture point where the material breaks after the peak. The shape and length of the curve reveal the ductility and toughness of the substance. A ductile material typically shows a long plastic region with significant strain before fracture. A short, steep curve characterizes a brittle substance. Key points like yield, ultimate strength, and fracture reveal the limits of the part. The curve shape reveals material properties. Accurate reading prevents the misuse of materials in industrial applications. What Do the Axes and Key Points Represent on the Graph? The axes and key points on a stress strain graph represent the fundamental mechanical properties and limits of a material. The y-axis represents stress, and the x-axis represents strain. The origin shows the state of the material before any load is applied. The initial linear slope represents Young's Modulus, which indicates the stiffness of the substance. Key points include yield strength, which is the limit of reversible deformation. Ultimate tensile strength is the peak of the curve, representing the maximum stress the material withstands. The fracture point marks the breaking stress and strain, representing the end of the test. Ductility is determined by the total strain at the moment of fracture. Toughness is represented by the total area under the curve. The markers are used by designers to set safety margins for mechanical parts. Accurate identification of the points prevents the overloading of structural systems. The graph serves as a tool for material comparison and engineering analysis. The points indicate material limits and guide the design process. Can a Stress-Strain Graph Predict Material Failure? Yes, a stress strain graph can predict material failure by identifying the critical points where a substance loses its structural integrity. The graph shows where failure occurs by marking the ultimate tensile strength and the final fracture point. The ultimate tensile strength indicates the maximum stress the material can withstand. Localized necking begins once the peak is passed, signaling imminent breakage. The fracture point marks the breaking stress where the material physically separates. Engineers use the values to establish safety factors, ensuring that the working stress stays below the failure limits. Monitoring the curve helps avoid dangerous load conditions that lead to sudden collapse. Brittle failure is predicted by a lack of a plastic region, while ductile failure is preceded by stretching. Accurate data from the graph allows for the prevention of accidents in construction and manufacturing. The diagram provides a reliable way to assess the risk of breakage in real-world applications. Engineers use the fracture point to avoid unsafe loads. What Are the Different Regions of the Stress-Strain Curve Graph? The different regions of the stress strain curve graph are the elastic, plastic, and fracture regions. Each region represents a distinct material response to the applied force. The elastic region is the initial phase where the material returns to its original shape upon unloading. The relationship between stress and strain is linear in the section. The plastic region follows the yield point and shows permanent deformation. Plastic deformation occurs primarily through dislocation motion within the crystal structure. Strain hardening and necking occur as the material nears its limit in the plastic region. The fracture region is the final part of the curve where the material breaks. Transitioning between these regions signals a behavioral change. Recognizing these phases helps engineers design structural systems that remain safe under peak loads. The diagram serves as a map to the performance of any substance. Precise identification of the regions prevents the misuse of materials in industrial applications. Each region represents a distinct material response. How Are Plastic and Fracture Regions Defined? The plastic and fracture regions are defined by the permanent change and final failure of a material. The plastic region starts immediately after the yield point, where the material can no longer return to its original shape. Plastic deformation in metals occurs primarily through dislocation motion, while polymers may deform through chain alignment and sliding. Elongation occurs significantly in the section of ductile materials. The plastic region includes the peak of the curve, known as the ultimate tensile strength. The fracture region begins after the ultimate strength is reached, and localized necking occurs. The engineering stress decreases after necking due to area reduction, while true stress may continue to increase. The fracture point itself is the coordinate where the specimen breaks into pieces. The regions are used to evaluate the ductility and toughness of a substance. Engineers analyze the plastic behavior to determine if a part provides a warning before failing. Fracture data is used for failure analysis and fracture mechanics. The total area in the regions determines the energy absorption capacity of the part. Does Each Region Indicate a Change in Material Behavior? Yes, each region of the stress strain curve reflects a different mechanical response and change in the internal behavior of the material. Elastic is reversible, plastic is permanent, and fracture is failure. The shift from one region to the next signals that the material has reached a physical limit. Strain hardening in the plastic region shows that the material becomes more resistant to further deformation. Necking indicates that the material has begun to fail locally due to area reduction. The fracture region marks the complete separation of the material structure. Each region reflects a different mechanical response and behavioral change. Recognizing these changes is critical in design to avoid permanent damage to parts. High-stress parts must remain in the elastic region to ensure long-term functionality. Safety margins are calculated based on the proximity of the operating load to the plastic transition. Proper understanding of these shifts prevents catastrophic failures in engineering systems. How Is a Stress-Strain Curve Made? A stress-strain curve is made during a tensile test by applying a controlled pulling force to a standardized specimen until fracture occurs. The universal testing machine grips the specimen at both ends and increases the load at a constant rate while measuring the applied force and the resulting elongation. The Universal Testing Machine (UTM) records force and displacement continuously throughout the test. The machine converts force into engineering stress by dividing the load by the original cross-sectional area of the specimen. The machine converts elongation into engineering strain by dividing the change in length by the original gauge length. The software plots stress on the vertical axis and strain on the horizontal axis in real time. The resulting stress-strain curve reveals key mechanical properties of the material. The initial linear region represents elastic deformation, where the material returns to its original shape after unloading. The curve then reaches the yield point, followed by plastic deformation, where permanent deformation occurs. The highest point on the curve indicates ultimate tensile strength, and the final drop marks fracture. What Testing Methods Are Used To Create a Stress-Strain Curve? Tensile testing is the primary method used to create a stress strain curve by pulling a sample until it breaks. The method provides detailed data on the elongation and strength of the substance. Compression testing is also used when the material is expected to support a heavy weight. Compression tests push the sample together to measure how the sample shortens and widens. Bending tests are used to determine the flexural properties of materials. The chosen test depends on the material type and its intended real-world application. Brittle materials are frequently tested in compression because the materials are prone to cracking in tension. Most testing methods use load cells, but deformation measurement methods vary (extensometers, LVDTs, optical systems, or angular sensors depending on the test). High-precision instruments ensure that the resulting curve reflects the performance of the substance. The data is used to develop safety protocols and material certifications. Reliable testing is a requirement for the production of safe and durable components. The chosen test depends on the material and application. Is Tensile Testing Required To Generate the Curve? No, tensile testing is not required to generate the most comprehensive stress strain curve for ductile materials. The procedure involves pulling a standardized sample until the sample reaches the point of fracture. Other mechanical tests, like compression or bending, generate stress strain data. The tensile test provides detailed information about the elongation and necking behavior. Industry standards define the specific requirements for conducting the test. The resulting diagram identifies the yield point, ultimate strength, and ductility of the substance. Tensile testing remains the industry standard since the test reveals properties difficult to measure in other loading modes. Engineering handbooks publish data derived from tensile experiments for design calculations. The data is plotted to form the characteristic curve used by engineers globally. Compression tests are commonly used for brittle materials, but ductile materials can also be tested in compression. The tensile test provides the baseline for characterizing the strength of metals and polymers. Precise execution of the test ensures the accuracy of the resulting material behavior model. How Are Stress-Strain Curves Used in Manufacturing and 3D Printing? Stress strain curves guide material selection and process optimization in manufacturing and additive manufacturing. Manufacturers use the graphs to determine if a material survives forming processes (stamping or forging). The curves help select the right filament or resin for functional parts in the field of 3D Printing. The diagrams allow engineers to predict how printed components behave under a load. Designers analyze the curves to optimize print settings (infill density or layer height) for maximum strength. The graphs help identify the anisotropy of printed parts where strength varies with the print direction. Better data from the curves leads to fewer print defects and failures. The data reduces waste and improves the reliability of the final part. Engineers rely on the diagrams to establish safety margins for custom components. Understanding the mechanical behavior of a material is a requirement for high-quality production. The data revealed by the curve ensures that parts remain functional throughout the service life. Reliable material characterization is a requirement for successful 3D Printing . How Do Engineers Apply Stress-Strain Data To Part Design? Engineers apply stress strain data to part design by determining the allowable stress for a given material. The yield strength from the graph sets the upper limit to loads to prevent permanent deformation. Working stress is calculated by applying a safety factor to the yield strength. The component remains in the linear elastic region during its entire operation. The modulus of elasticity is used to calculate the stiffness and deflection of beams or supports. Ductility data helps in designing parts that absorb energy without sudden failure. Toughness values are used for components subjected to impact loads (car bumpers). Designers use the data to select the appropriate thickness and shape of a part for a specific weight. Accurate application of the curve properties prevents structural collapse. Stress-strain data is input into simulation software to test designs digitally. Refining the part before physical prototypes are built is possible with the data. Precise engineering design depends on the accurate interpretation of the material behavior curve. It prevents structural failure in real applications. Can Stress-Strain Curves Reduce Print Failures? Yes, stress strain curves can reduce print failures by helping optimize material and process settings in additive manufacturing. The graphs reveal the mechanical behavior of a material after testing, which can then be used to predict weaknesses before printing. Engineers use the data to determine if a specific filament or resin possesses enough strength for the intended application. The curves show the limit of safe load. The data prevents the accidental design of weak parts. Understanding the mechanical behavior allows designers to adjust infill patterns and orientation to improve part durability. Better data from testing leads to fewer print defects like cracking or delamination. Identifying the yield point helps set realistic service expectations for custom parts. Pre-testing materials provides a reliable way to avoid structural failure in real-world use. Continuous monitoring of material properties ensures a higher success rate for complex prints. Designers use the information to create components that remain stable under peak loads. It prevents the loss of time and resources associated with failed prints. Why Is Stress-Strain Data Important for CAD? Stress strain data is important for modern engineering software. Designers input the properties (Young's modulus and yield strength) into the software to perform structural analysis. Computerized tools use the information for finite element analysis (FEA) to predict how a part deforms under pressure. The simulation identifies potential failure points before a physical prototype is made. Accurate material data improves the reliability of the design, providing a realistic model of performance. Missing information can make simulations inaccurate and potentially misleading, increasing design risk. Structural and fatigue analysis depend on the precise coordinates of the stress-strain relationship. The data helps optimize the weight and shape of a component. Engineers rely on the simulations to save time and reduce manufacturing costs. Reliable modeling reduces the risk of parts failing in service. Accurate data is a requirement for Computer-Aided Design (CAD) Modeling . Realistic simulation of material behavior is possible with accurate data points. Modern design tools depend on the precise coordinates of the stress-strain relationship to produce safe components. How Is Stress-Strain Data Used in CAD? Stress strain data is input into simulation and finite element analysis tools in the digital design environment. The software uses the mathematical relationship between stress and strain to model the behavior of a part under load. Engineers define the material properties in the CAD environment using data derived from laboratory tests. The system calculates the distribution of stress across the geometry of the component. CAD predicts deformation and identifies areas where the stress exceeds the yield limit. The data allows designers to refine the shape and thickness of the part to avoid localized failure. Thermal stress analysis uses the data to predict changes due to temperature shifts. High-fidelity simulations require the full stress-strain curve for non-linear analysis. Accurate modeling helps select the safest material for the job. The data helps refine designs before manufacturing starts. Structural health and performance are validated digitally using the curve data. This helps in predicting deformation under load. Can Incorrect Material Data Cause Design Failure? Yes, incorrect material data can cause catastrophic design failure in engineering and manufacturing. Wrong data leads to weak designs appearing safe in a computer simulation but failing in reality. The part undergoes unexpected permanent deformation if the yield strength is overestimated. Underestimating the brittleness of a substance causes a sudden breakage without warning. Structural components must be designed with appropriate safety factors and validated data. Faulty data leads to the selection of a material that cannot handle the operational loads. Inaccurate testing results in the creation of parts that are too heavy or too weak. Accurate testing is a requirement for safe engineering. Precise material characterization is necessary for safe and reliable engineering. Designers must verify the accuracy of the data used in the calculations. Structural integrity depends on the quality of the information provided by material tests. High-quality data is necessary for the prevention of accidents and the success of any engineering project. How Are Stress-Strain Curves Used? Stress strain curves are used to evaluate material strength and ductility in a wide range of engineering applications. Engineers rely on the diagrams for safety and performance calculations in construction, aerospace, and automotive design. The graphs guide the selection of materials providing objective data on the mechanical behavior. Manufacturers use the curves to set limits to forming and machining processes. Quality control departments use the data to verify that batches of material meet the required standards. Forensic engineers analyze the curves to understand why a structure failed during service. The diagrams are used to develop new alloys and polymers with improved properties. Academic researchers use the information to teach the principles of materials science. Precise plotting of the data points is necessary for accurate structural analysis. The graphs serve as a universal language for describing material performance. Understanding the relationship between stress and strain is necessary for modern engineering. The information provided by the curve ensures the safety of everyone using the final product. How Do Engineers Use Stress-Strain Curves in Design? Engineers use stress strain curves in design to select the most appropriate material based on the mechanical behavior. Engineers set load limits and safety margins by referring to the yield and ultimate tensile strengths on the graph. The elastic region helps in calculating the stiffness needed for parts like springs or aircraft wings. Toughness data from the area under the curve is used for parts that must resist impact. Ductility values guide the design of components that need to bend without snapping. High-stress environments require materials with high ultimate strength. Portable devices use the data to select lightweight materials that remain rigid. Stress-strain curves provide material behavior, but lifespan prediction requires fatigue data (S-N curves) and time-dependent analysis. Accurate interpretation of the curve ensures the durability and structural integrity of the component. This ensures that products remain safe and functional for the intended use. Detailed material data is a requirement for building reliable and high-performance structural systems. Can Stress-Strain Curves Prevent Material Failure? Yes, stress strain curves can prevent material failure by identifying the critical failure points of a substance. They show the maximum allowable stress before a part undergoes permanent deformation or breakage. Engineers design structures that always remain in the safe elastic region by knowing the yield strength. The diagrams provide a map of how much stress a material can withstand before failing. It identifies the moment when the risk of fracture increases. Understanding these limits helps in setting realistic service conditions for any given part. Proper use of the data reduces the risk of breakage during unexpected peak loads. Designers apply safety factors based on the data to create a buffer against failure. Monitoring material properties ensures that the components perform as intended. Accurate visualization of the mechanical limits prevents the accidental overloading of critical structures. It helps engineers create durable products that protect the public. Reliability in engineering is built on the precise application of the properties revealed by the curve. What Is the Difference Between Engineering Stress-Strain and True Stress-Strain? Engineering stress-strain and true stress-strain represent two ways to describe material behavior. Engineering stress uses the original cross-sectional area of the specimen in the calculation. The method is simple and common in design since the initial area is easy to measure. True stress uses the actual instantaneous cross-sectional area as the area thins during stretching. True stress accounts for necking in materials and provides accuracy at high levels of deformation. Engineering strain compares the change in length to the original length. True strain measures the continuous change based on the instantaneous length of the specimen. Engineering stress loses accuracy near the fracture point since the area reduces significantly. True stress shows that the material becomes stronger than the engineering curve suggests. Understanding the variations is a requirement for advanced structural analysis. Engineers prefer true stress to modeling metal forming or high-deformation processes. Precise calculations help predict failure in ductile metals. The study clarifies Stress vs. Strain: What Are the Key Differences? . How Are Engineering and True Stress-Strain Calculated? Engineering stress is calculated by dividing the applied force by the original cross-sectional area of the sample. The corresponding engineering strain is found by dividing the change in length by the original length. The calculations are straightforward and serve as the basis for standard mechanical testing reports. True stress is calculated by dividing the applied force by the actual cross-sectional area at the specific moment. The process requires monitoring the instantaneous diameter of the specimen during the test. True strain is found by taking the natural logarithm of the ratio between the current length and the original length. The method provides a precise measurement of continuous deformation with high precision. True stress strain data is necessary for accurate simulations of manufacturing processes like rolling or deep drawing. True stress equals engineering stress multiplied by one plus engineering strain, and true strain equals the natural logarithm of one plus engineering strain (valid before necking). Accurate measurements are necessary to understand the behavior of materials beyond the yield point. These calculations ensure the material model remains realistic under large deformations. Is True Stress-Strain More Accurate at High Deformation? Yes, true stress-strain is highly accurate at high deformation near fracture. It accounts for the reduction in cross-sectional area that occurs during stretching and necking. Engineering stress tends to underestimate the actual intensity of the internal forces because the formula assumes the area remains constant. True stress more accurately represents the actual stress state in the material based on instantaneous geometry. The level of precision is necessary for modeling manufacturing processes. title: Fillet vs. Chamfer — What Are the Differences and Uses?
summary: Learn about what sets them apart and use cases for each
body_text: When you’re designing joining parts, the smaller details are just as important as the larger portions. Something as minuscule as an edge is a big determining factor in how smoothly two parts fit together or move off one another. That’s especially true for edge styles, like fillet and chamfer, which each bring their own benefits and greatly improve the joining and movement of two or more parts. Edges like these provide two important features — an easier joining experience and reduced stress on certain areas of a part. A chamfer is helpful when you need to buffer the sharp change in direction, as it’s cut into an angled slope. Alternatively, a fillet is most useful if you need a smooth, curved edge to join two surfaces together, and it’s important for reducing the stress concentration that shows up in corners of a part or mating parts that are joined together, whether you’re machining small batches of products or rapid machining large quantities of mating components. Below, we explore specific details about how a fillet and chamfer work and when you’d use each style. What is a Fillet? Visually, a fillet edge is a smooth curve that waterfalls from the top of a part to the side. Engineers and designers can create this rounded style of edge for the interior or exterior of a part, and it’s handy in reducing pressure on tools or components that bear heavy loads. This type of edge is a popular solution when you’re casting, machining, molding, and 3D printing objects because the smooth design makes it easier for parts to slide around in comparison to leaving sharp edges on an object. The two most common ways of crafting a fillet edge is through machining a radial tool path or 3D printing one. The first involves cutting a path between two surfaces on your object with machining tools, whereas the second gets designing through a software program and is set to create this type of surface during the 3D printing process. What Is the Purpose of a Fillet? When there is a change of direction or sections on a part, a fillet edge helps reduce the stress that comes with this switch. Its smooth, rounded edge creates less friction and takes a load off certain areas. This in turn means your parts won’t fatigue as quickly and it raises their load-bearing capacity. When it comes to reducing this stress, you’ll likely rely on a fillet edge over a chamfer for this purpose. What Does a Filleted Edge Look Like? A fillet edge provides a little more than just function — it also helps boost the aesthetics of a part, since its edges are softer and rounded. The appearance of this edge on a part looks concave and rounded on interior surfaces, and unsurprisingly, convex and rounded on exterior corners. A fillet makes for a finish that looks seamless from all angles. However, one thing to bear in mind is that fillets can increase manufacturing time for subtractive processes, such as CNC machining, so incorporating them into your design simply for aesthetics may come at a higher cost. You may find that a beveled edge reminds you of a fillet edge, but the two are not the same. A fillet is rounded, whereas a bevel is a diagonal cut. The latter is usually used when you need to weld or permanently seal two parts together for a strong joint. How Are Fillets Specified in AutoCAD®? Making a fillet in AutoCAD® is done by using the “FILLET” command. Select two lines in your design that meet at an interior or exterior corner. Enter the size of the radius that will form the fillet. Once a value has been prescribed, AutoCAD® will automatically adjust the length of the selected lines, generate the fillet, and remove the sharp corner. Does a Filleted Edge Look More Appealing? Yes, filleted edges look more appealing. Fillets can be desired for interior surfaces because they create a seamless surface that is blended together. They may be desired for exterior surfaces because they remove potentially dangerous sharp corners and burrs. What Is a Chamfer? Another edge style to know is a chamfer. Its design features an angle or slope between two surfaces of a part that’s flat, as opposed to the fillet edge’s rounded surface. It’s also one option for improving the movement and joining of two or several parts. However, you probably wouldn’t choose a chamfer edge over a fillet style when it comes to reducing high levels of stress. Instead, they’re a great choice for assembling mating parts, especially at a 45-degree angle — though you can really customize them for any angle of your choosing. Chamfers can be machined, like fillets, and they can be cut by hand. You can also design them in CAD programs, which makes it easier for certain machines or 3D printers to produce when it has already been programmed into the design. You’ll find they’re simpler to cut, too, because there isn’t a radius involved, like with a fillet. This fact also makes them a bit more economical to produce than fillets, so if you're simply looking to break a sharp edge, you may want to consider chamfers. What Is the Purpose of a Chamfer? Like a fillet, a chamfer edge also helps buffer the original sharp edges of a part, making assembly easier for mating components. You can choose from a variety of sizes and angles and lean on a single chamfer tool, countersink, or spot drill to make it. What Does a Chamfered Edge Look Like? You’ll notice a chamfer looks like a ramp or slanted surface and it will connect the top of a part to another side. When learning about the look and style of a chamfer, you might also think of a tapered edge, but there is a difference. A tapered edge is a gradual reduction in a specific dimension over the length of an object, whereas a chamfer is an edge style that’s only applied between two surfaces of a part. How Is Chamfer in AutoCAD®? Chamfers are created in AutoCAD® using the “CHAMFER” command. Type “CHAMFER” in the command line, then select the two lines in the design that will be connected by the chamfer. Specify the length of the flat face section or the angles of the chamfer, and AutoCAD® will automatically remove the sharp edge and generate the chamfer. To learn more, see our full guide on AutoCAD vs. SolidWorks . Does a Chamfer Cost Less than a Fillet? Yes, the cost of fabricating a chamfer costs less than creating a fillet. This is because chamfers don’t require the same levels of precision as cutting a radius or fillet. The tool paths for creating chamfers are more straightforward. Additionally, different-sized chamfers can be created with a single tool, unlike fillets that may require multiple tools to cut a single radius. Does a Chamfer's Angle Have To Be 45 degrees? No, chamfer angles are not required to be 45 degrees. Chamfers can be specified at any angle and can also be specified by the length of the face. When to Know if You Need Fillet or Chamfer? You’ve learned that both fillet and chamfer edges have their own style and benefits, but let’s go more in-depth about situations when you’d want to select one or the other: Instances in which you’d want to use a fillet edge include: Parts that will bear heavy loads: Fillet edges are best when it comes to parts that will be under pressure or carry heavy loads as they reduce stress — something that a chamfer doesn’t do as well. Parts will be presented or seen: A fillet edge provides an aesthetically pleasing finish, therefore if you’ll be showing a specific part or it will be on display, this could be a good reason to settle on this edge style. Benefits outweigh the cost: Fillet edges are more expensive to create, but if you find after some analysis that your parts require the benefits only a fillet edge can provide, it’s better to opt for this edge type. Alternatively, the situations in which you’d want to use a chamfer edge include: Heavy loads won’t be involved: Unlike a fillet, chamfer edges aren’t well-equipped to handle heavy loads, so it’s best to understand how much weight or pressure you’ll expose the parts to. Mating parts are involved: To get the smoothest connection and movement between two mating parts, chamfer edges are the way to go, whether it’s for a pin, bolt, drive screw, or something completely different. Cost efficiency is important: When you compare these two edges, you’ll find that chamfered edges are cheaper to make than fillets since the former can be machined with simple tools in one motion rather than requiring more specialized tools or ones that require multiple sweeps to shape out curves. If a fillet’s benefits aren’t necessary, a chamfer will be more cost-efficient. Knowing about these two styles of edges will make it easier to choose the right finish when it comes to combining parts of tools and machinery. Both fillet and chamfer edges offer unique purposes, it’s just a matter of considering what will serve the final product best in the end. What Are the Differences Between Fillets and Chamfers? Now that you understand what both a fillet and chamfer look like and how they’re used, let’s break down their three main differences. Their visual appearance: A fillet edge is smooth and rounded, whereas you’ll see that a chamfer edge is angled, but they both connect two surfaces together. Their purposes: While both are made to ease up on sharp edges, a fillet edge is most helpful in reducing stress on parts that bear heavy loads, whereas a chamfer edge is ideal for joining mating parts. Their costs: A fillet edge is more expensive to manufacture because it involves cutting a radius and rounded edge, whereas a chamfer is a straight, angled edge. The image below will give you an idea of how they compare visually and shows a sketch of two cubes, one with a fillet edge on the left and the other on the right with chamfered edges. Fillet edge (left) vs. a chamfered edge (right) Frequently Asked Questions About Fillets and Chamfers Do Fillets Result in Stronger Edges Than Chamfers? Yes, a fillet is a stronger edge design than a chamfer. They make parts more visually appealing than chamfers and safer because there is no edge. Fillets also greatly increase the load-bearing capability and fatigue resistance of a part. This is because fillets allow stresses to be more evenly distributed across an interior or exterior edge. Is a Chamfer the Same As a Taper? No, a chamfer is not the same as a taper. A taper is a gradual reduction in a dimension over a particular length. Chamfers are applied only at the edge where two surfaces of a part meet. Is a Fillet the Same As a Bevel? No, a fillet is not the same as a bevel. Fillets are rounded edges between two adjacent surfaces, while bevels are diagonal cuts that join two parallel surfaces. Bevels are most often used on parts that are to be welded together. Bevels allow a significant amount of surface area for molten metal to bond to the two halves of a workpiece, which makes for a strong and effective joint. To learn more, see our full guide on Bevel . How Xometry Can Help Whether you decide to use fillets, chamfers, or a combination of both in your part designs, Xometry can handle either with ease. As we mentioned in the sections above, cost can be a consideration between the two. With the Xometry Instant Quoting Engine® you can easily compare the costs of both edge conditions. Try quoting a machined part with chamfered edges, and then do the same for a version with fillets. The pricing and lead time differences will be revealed within seconds, allowing you to make the most informed decision. body_text: Welcome back to the Apollo Changelog. After taking a week off, we’re back with a fresh batch of news for you! A glimpse into Apollo’s monorepo Ever wonder how GraphOS works under the hood?
